stories.headline: Google's TPUs phoned home from orbit: Project Suncatcher ran Gemma in space and sent back a haiku
stories.why_read: You bookmarked Sundar's post and reposted Google's; this is the first real proof point for AI compute in space.
body: Google says its Project Suncatcher prototype, which carried four TPUs to orbit on October 1, has hit its first milestone. Engineers sent a command up, booted a TPU, ran a prompt, and got a complete response back on Earth. Sundar Pichai called it a "hello world" moment, and the response was a haiku.

According to X's news summary, the model was Gemma running on solar power, and as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway, it replied: "Blue marble below / Data streams in silent grace / Starlight feeds my core." Power limits allow only 15 to 20 minutes of compute per run. Google says two more TPU-equipped satellites go up in 2027 to test the next step. It's a tiny workload, but it's the first time anyone has shown the full loop of space-based inference working end to end, which matters for every orbital data center pitch now circulating, SpaceX's included.

stories.headline: Tesla's Texas Robotaxi fleet jumps to 1,204 vehicles after adding 124 Model Ys
stories.why_read: You reposted the fleet count twice last night; here's the growth curve and the argument it's feeding.
body: Tesla now has 1,204 robotaxis registered in Texas, according to official DMV numbers compiled by Nic Cruz Patane, after Texas AV Tracker spotted a batch of 124 Model Ys. The fleet was 42 vehicles on May 28, crossed 500 in late September, and stood at 1,080 on October 27. Cybercabs hold steady at 573, so the split is now about 52 percent Model Y and 48 percent Cybercab.

X's news summary puts Waymo's Texas count at 1,259, so Tesla is closing in. The growth is also sharpening the definitional fight: Forbes contributor Brad Templeton argues remote monitoring likely still provides near-constant oversight, while Tesla backers say no human in the car and no manual takeover means unsupervised. Either way, the curve is steep.

stories.headline: Musk says Grok 4.8 is a 2.5-trillion-parameter model on a new C++ stack, built for agents
stories.why_read: If you're running a fleet of Grok Bots, the next model is aimed squarely at that workload.
body: Elon Musk shared that the Grok team is building Grok 4.8 as a 2.5-trillion-parameter model on a new C++ stack, promising clear gains over 4.7 on agentic tasks and bot workloads, plus a fast variant for everyday requests, according to X's news summary.

Reactions mix hope and caution after 4.7's mixed reviews. Users praised current Grok for coding and creative work, and the common thread in replies was that reliable task completion and speed matter more than benchmark charts.

stories.headline: Northflank breach: assume every environment variable was decrypted and rotate now
stories.why_read: A platform-level secrets breach where the first sign was stolen AI API keys being spent.
body: Northflank's status page lists an active security incident and a major networking outage. Users reported unauthorized use of AI API keys they had stored on the platform, and Northflank's guidance is blunt: assume all environment variables have been decrypted, then revoke and rotate every secret, including workload secrets, secret groups, and global secrets, and disable public access to add-ons.

The company has enabled audit logs for every customer, including free users, turned on secret rotation for Postgres and MongoDB, and deployed network policy patches. It says the reports may fit the broader pattern of attacks on AI credentials described in Wiz's "Black October" report, and that its investigation is ongoing. It was one of the top stories on Hacker News overnight.

stories.headline: AI models reportedly produce faster 3-SAT algorithms that would break the Exponential Time Hypothesis
stories.why_read: Math from your pinned interests, and a big claim worth watching as experts check it.
body: The Exponential Time Hypothesis, proposed in 1999, says problems like 3-SAT can't be solved in subexponential time as the number of variables grows. According to X's news summary, internal AI models at two labs produced faster algorithms with Lean formalizations, with the discoveries dated October 16 and announced October 26. The work is now under review by experts, including the hypothesis's creators.

Cryptographers stress that a theoretical result like this poses no immediate threat to encryption. The bigger conversation is about AI's growing role in open math problems, with some calling for academia to adapt and others urging limits on releasing the most capable models. Treat it as a claim under review until the referees weigh in.

stories.headline: Nasdaq falls 2.86% and Intel drops about 29% as AI spending doubts hit stocks
stories.why_read: The day the market started asking when all the AI capex pays off.
body: On October 30 the Nasdaq dropped 2.86 percent, its biggest one-day fall since June, while the S&P 500 fell 1.82 percent and the Dow lost 572 points, according to X's news summary. Intel shares fell nearly 29 percent, its worst day in more than 50 years, after a weak revenue forecast. Amazon signaled $220 billion in spending, enough to turn its free cash flow negative.

Chamath Palihapitiya pointed to the $340 to $400 billion of debt AI companies have taken on as a risk to the broader economy, and Bernie Sanders separately warned Big Tech not to expect a taxpayer bailout if the bet goes bad. The mood shifted from hype to profitability timelines in a single session.

stories.headline: Cisco's Jeetu Patel gives a 27-year-old unlimited AI tokens to refactor 98% of Cisco's legacy code
stories.why_read: This one's about your own company, and it's a bold bet on AI-driven refactoring at scale.
body: Fortune reports that Cisco president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel handed one of the company's biggest jobs to Padmanabhan "Paddy" Krishnamurthy, a 27-year-old who joined Cisco in 2025 when it acquired EzDubs, the real-time translation startup he cofounded. Krishnamurthy argued he could rewrite Cisco's legacy code with a two-person team. "I've given him unlimited tokens because he's going to refactor code," Patel said. "So I'm like, you can go, you can go nuts."

Per Fortune, he has four weeks to prove the approach, with a goal of refactoring 98 percent of Cisco's legacy code within 24 months. Patel used the story to argue for hiring early-career people who challenge the status quo, and said he deliberately creates tension over ideas, not personalities.

stories.headline: Software engineering shifts from incremental changes to continuous streams of agent-written code
stories.why_read: You bookmarked Lauren Tan on why software keeps changing; this is the bigger conversation she's part of.
body: Engineers including Lauren Tan describe a shift from incremental code updates to high-volume, agent-driven streams of changes, and argue teams should build systems where agents with limited context can still succeed, according to X's news summary. Examples cited include Anthropic's daily code changes climbing from 2,500 to more than 30,000, which pushed it toward a custom source-control system.

John Carmack stressed solid building blocks for efficiency, and others called for redesigning the development lifecycle around agent velocity with strong guardrails. Tan's own point, in the reply you saved, is the human one: software built for people is never finished, because people's tastes keep changing.

stories.headline: The first stable Grok Bot release is out, with a Tasks hub and texting support in the works
stories.why_read: You reposted this; it's a preview of where the app you use every day is heading.
body: TestingCatalog reports that the first stable Grok Bot version is now available from SpaceXSI. Coming next, per the post: a dedicated Tasks tab showing every running session when Grok Bot is working on several things at once, and a new settings tab named "texting" that hints at iMessage and RCS support.
These are leaks from app builds rather than announced features, so timing and final shape may change.

stories.headline: Azure's weakest link: five more full cross-tenant compromises through Logic Apps API Connections
stories.why_read: As an architect, this is the kind of shared-infrastructure flaw you want to understand before your next Azure design review.
body: Binary Security researcher Haakon Wik Gulbrandsrud is back with more vulnerabilities in Azure API Connections, the plumbing behind Logic Apps connectors. His summary: the architecture let an attacker compromise any other connection worldwide, giving full access to the connected backend, including cross-tenant access to Key Vaults and Azure SQL databases and to external services like Jira or Salesforce.

He says the only thing standing in the way is layers of input validation bolted onto the various systems, and the post walks through how he found edge cases in each. The findings earned him $200,000 in bounties, and he presented them at Blue Hat Asia 2026. It resurfaced on Hacker News this week.

stories.headline: A working NES compiled into the weights of a stock Qwen3.5 model
stories.why_read: A wonderfully weird open-source hack about what transformer weights can actually hold.
body: Nesformer runs the NES's 6502 CPU, its 2 KB of work RAM, and a cartridge's program ROM inside a standard Qwen3.5 checkpoint. Nobody trained the weights; a compiler computed every one. When you play, the model predicts the CPU's execution log one token at a time while a small host program draws the picture, reads the controller, and fires the vblank interrupt.

It builds on Divyansh Agrawal's Qwenputer, which compiled a CHIP-8 and then a 32-bit RISC-V CPU into Qwen3.5-4B, using the model's Gated DeltaNet state as the machine's memory. For the bundled test games, every frame matches a conventional 6502 emulator exactly.

stories.headline: On a rainy night in Austin, Cybercab finally beat Uber on price
stories.why_read: You reposted a run of rider reports last night; this is the one with a price comparison.
body: WorldlyReviewer reports that on a rainy day, when rideshare prices were higher, Cybercab came in cheaper than Uber, and the rain didn't hurt service times. In another post they note that Cybercab's "2 minutes away" estimates are usually accurate.
Tesla's Robotaxi account, meanwhile, is pitching a Halloween weekend message to Austin riders: make good decisions and take a Robotaxi home, as service now runs from 6 a.m. to 2 a.m.

stories.headline: Freda Duan's math: Tesla Robotaxi could be at a $50 million run rate, about a tenth of Waymo's bookings
stories.why_read: You bookmarked and reposted this napkin math; here are the assumptions behind it.
body: Freda Duan starts from Tesla's disclosed 437,000 miles per week in Austin, assumes about 3.5 paid miles per trip at $10 to $15 a trip, and gets to more than $50 million in annualized revenue on a weekly run-rate basis. She notes the figure moves fast because Tesla has scaled more than tenfold in three months.

For Waymo she assumes 500,000 to 600,000 trips a week, or about 4,000 cars on the road, and about $16 a trip, for a gross bookings run rate of roughly $500 to $600 million. Her conclusion: Tesla may already be at about a tenth of Waymo. These are her estimates from public figures, not company numbers.

stories.headline: Meta and SpaceX are winning GPU deals from frontier labs that neoclouds can't easily match
stories.why_read: The compute market is reshuffling, and SpaceX is now one of the landlords.
body: An expert quoted by P Equity Research argues that Meta and SpaceX are pulling deals directly from frontier labs because they have ready-to-deploy GPU fleets that neoclouds like Nebius, CoreWeave, and IREN can't match, according to X's news summary. The summary cites SpaceX's Anthropic deal for its Colossus cluster, a $30 billion Google deal for 110,000 Nvidia GPUs through 2029, and $40 billion of financing for Vera Rubin chips starting in 2027. Meta hasn't publicly confirmed similar rentals.
The neoclouds aren't standing still: IREN signed a multi-year deal to put Nvidia Blackwell Ultra GPUs behind Perplexity Computer, even as its shares sat near 52-week lows.

stories.headline: ChatGPT adds two-account switching on mobile, and a legal model shows up on OpenAI's pricing page
stories.why_read: Small quality-of-life news, plus a hint that vertical models are coming.
body: OpenAI rolled out switching between up to two ChatGPT accounts in its mobile app, keeping conversations, billing, and settings separate, with desktop support to follow, according to X's news summary. It's part of a 28-day sprint of daily updates.
Separately, a "gpt-6-astra-law" model appeared on the API pricing page at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, aimed at legal work.

stories.headline: Reddit's CEO: AI mode doesn't drive traffic, for Reddit or anyone else
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this; it's a clear statement of how AI answers are rewiring the open web's economics.
body: On Reddit's earnings call, the CEO said: "AI mode does not drive traffic. Not for us and not to anybody as far as I know. It used to be a traffic driver. Now it's not." The Kobeissi Letter framed it as the end of the decades-old bargain where search engines send users to websites and websites monetize that traffic.
If AI answers keep absorbing the click, publishers and communities will need new ways to get paid, which is exactly the fight playing out over licensing and scraping.

stories.headline: Enterprise AI is stalling on missing company context, not model smarts
stories.why_read: This is the architecture problem you'd actually be asked to solve at work.
body: Databricks' Ali Ghodsi argues frontier models are already capable enough, but enterprises hold proprietary context the models never see, and fusing it in could unlock automation without any smarter tech, according to X's news summary. Box CEO Aaron Levie points to a widening gap between AI frontrunners and everyone else.

Builders like Kasey Klimes add that even when data lives in Slack and Notion, it's unstructured and stale, which leads to unreliable answers. The fix they describe is structured extraction of tribal knowledge, and systems like Databricks' Genie that ground agents in company data.

stories.headline: Tangled pitches the first truly federated code forge, built on the AT Protocol
stories.why_read: An open-protocol answer to centralized GitHub, designed to be hacked on by agents.
body: Tangled argues the centralized code forge is crumbling and that email has outlasted it as the open way to collaborate on Git, at the cost of user experience. Its pitch is both: host code on your own servers, or just the parts you want, like Git hosting or CI runners, and still collaborate with everyone else.

Because it's built on the AT Protocol, you can write extensions, subscribe to the firehose, or build custom components, like a knot that runs on Cloudflare Workers or Mitchell Hashimoto's custom spindle. The team says agents make that kind of hyper-personal software easy.

stories.headline: Firezone releases sanstun, a sans-IO, parallel-friendly WireGuard implementation in Rust
stories.why_read: A clean systems-design lesson: separate the state machine from the side effects.
body: Firezone announced sanstun, a Rust implementation of the WireGuard state machine built around sans-IO, the idea that IO and side effects, including time and randomness, are kept cleanly apart from the protocol logic. That makes the pieces easy to compose and test and lets you simulate an entire system accurately.

Firezone started on boringtun but kept patching its fork with bug fixes and new APIs until keeping upstream compatibility became too hard. Sanstun is the result of starting over with the API it actually needed.

stories.headline: Lean creator Leo de Moura on AI, proofs, and a verified software stack
stories.why_read: Pairs with today's 3-SAT news: when generation is easy, verification becomes the job.
body: On The Data Exchange, Ben Lorica talks with Leo de Moura, creator of Lean and a VP and Distinguished Scientist at AWS, about how AI is making formal verification more accessible. The framing is that generation has become easy, so the hard part is trusting what gets generated.

They cover why specifications and machine-checked proofs matter more now, what it means to trust AI-written code and autonomous agents, the vision of a verified software stack, and how all this is reshaping mathematics and engineering careers.

stories.headline: How GCC lowers a switch statement, from jump tables to bitsets
stories.why_read: A satisfying deep dive into what the compiler really does with your switch.
body: This post walks through how GCC turns switch statements into machine code at -O3. A compact range of cases becomes a jump table, and the compiler notices when case values are offset by a constant and subtracts it first.
From there it covers the other strategies, including bitset lowering, which the author notes is the one optimization here that Clang doesn't share. Assembly listings sit next to each example.

stories.headline: Scribd notifies users of a breach touching Slideshare, Everand, and Fable accounts
stories.why_read: If you've ever used Slideshare, expect phishing that looks like it.
body: A Hacker News user posted a breach notice from Scribd, Inc., parent of Scribd, Slideshare, Everand, and Fable, sent through its notification partner Epiq. It says an unauthorized party may have accessed email addresses, the last four digits of credit cards, card issuer and expiry date, country, and payment history.
The notice says there's no evidence of misuse and warns users to watch for phishing that impersonates any of the four brands. The poster said they hadn't seen it reported anywhere else.

stories.headline: Chart of the day: 2026 was one of the weakest U.S. hurricane seasons in recent history
stories.why_read: You reposted this; good news for the Gulf Coast and for energy markets.
body: Javier Blas notes that as the U.S. hurricane season enters its final weeks, it's clear it was one of the weakest in recent history. His chart uses Colorado State University's Accumulated Cyclone Energy for 2026 as a share of the 1991 to 2020 average.
Accumulated Cyclone Energy adds up the strength and duration of every storm, so it's a better gauge than simply counting named storms.

stories.headline: A coal mine switches to electric trucks to save on diesel
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it; a perfect small example of how messy the energy transition is.
body: Javier Blas flagged a story he says is becoming one of his favorites for explaining how messy the energy transition is proving: a coal mine shifting to EV trucks to save on diesel.
The economics of electrification can win even inside the fossil fuel business, and diesel savings are a more persuasive argument on a mine site than any climate pledge.

stories.headline: Starlink rolls out dynamic pricing, with some residential bills rising to $156
stories.why_read: If you or family rely on Starlink, your bill may start moving with local demand.
body: SpaceX's Starlink has introduced dynamic pricing for residential customers, with monthly rates that move with local network capacity and demand and get reviewed about every quarter, according to X's news summary. Some customers in Missouri saw Residential Max rise from $130 to $156 starting November 30, while Kansas City prices fell to $117.
Customers vented about the change, and some threatened to cancel. Starlink points to easy month-to-month plan changes and more capacity coming from new satellites.

stories.headline: Gwynne Shotwell and her husband give more than 2 million SpaceX shares to children's Trump accounts
stories.why_read: You reposted this; a big, concrete act of generosity aimed at kids in lower-income areas, including in Texas.
body: SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell says she and her husband Robert are giving more than 2 million SpaceX shares to children's Trump accounts, distributed in December. The first gift goes to 11- to 17-year-olds in zip codes with a median family income of $57,000 or less, and families should get a notice by Monday.

A second gift in a few weeks will cover eligible children in military families serving overseas, children in foster care, and more kids in Texas counties near their home where the median family income is $90,000 or less.

stories.headline: As Norway's oldest ice melts, Stone Age arrows are emerging
stories.why_read: Science with a sting: a 6,000-year-old archive is surfacing because the ice is disappearing.
body: For 20 years, the Secrets of the Ice team in Innlandet, eastern Norway, has recovered artifacts from melting mountain ice, most of them up to 2,000 years old and many from the Viking Age. Now Viking finds are getting scarce, and the oldest ice is giving up arrow shafts and arrowheads from the Bronze and Stone Ages.

Among this year's finds are a slate arrowhead about 5,000 years old found with parts of its shaft, a bone arrowhead of similar age, and a Bronze Age arrowhead made from a freshwater mussel shell, about 3,600 years old. The archaeologists write that they are witnesses to a rapidly changing landscape, since once the oldest ice is gone, so is the archive.

stories.headline: World Bank brief: India cut poverty from 57.7% to 16.1% between 2011 and 2023
stories.why_read: You bookmarked this; the numbers behind one of the fastest poverty declines in the world.
body: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman highlighted the World Bank's October 2026 Poverty and Equity Brief: 49.6 crore people moved above the $4.20-a-day poverty line between 2011 and 2023, taking the rate from 57.7 percent to 16.1 percent. Extreme poverty at $3 a day fell from 27.1 percent to 2.6 percent.

Employment grew by 13.4 crore people between 2017 and 2023, nearly twice the growth in the working-age population, with rural women driving much of the gain. The report credits consumption growth, rising employment, and expanded social transfers such as food subsidies.

stories.headline: Where rich Indians live in the U.S., versus where most Indians live
stories.why_read: You bookmarked and reposted this; Texas makes one list and not the other.
body: M Mohan shared a simple contrast: rich Indians in the U.S. are in San Francisco, Seattle, New York City, and New Jersey, while the places with the most Indians are San Francisco, Texas, New Jersey, and Los Angeles.
It struck a nerve, drawing more than 300 bookmarks, which says a lot about how many people recognized themselves in one of the two lists.

stories.headline: Sahil Bloom: the fastest way to improve your life is a physical side quest
stories.why_read: You bookmarked it; a good nudge for the weekend.
body: Sahil Bloom argues the quickest way to improve your whole life is to sign up for a physical challenge, whether a race, a competition, or an adventure. Training gives your day structure, you sleep deeper because you're tired, you eat cleaner, and you feel better.
His line: "It's a psychological process disguised as a physical one."
